claims.text: Individuals in the highest quantile of sugar-sweetened beverage intake have a 26% greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared to those in the lowest quantile.
Higher consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with an increased risk of metabolic syndrome.

evidence.description: Meta-analysis of 8 studies including 310,819 participants and 15,043 cases showed a relative risk of 1.26 (95% CI 1.12-1.41) comparing highest to lowest intake quantiles.
Meta-analysis of 3 studies including 19,431 participants and 5,803 cases yielded a pooled relative risk of 1.20 (95% CI 1.02-1.42).

methodologies.name: Random-effects meta-analysis
methodologies.description: A random-effects meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies from MEDLINE database up to May 2010 evaluating SSB intake and risk of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes.
conditions: Highest quantile of SSB intake (1-2 servings/day) versus lowest quantile (none or <1 serving/month)

limitations.text: The role of SSBs in the development of chronic metabolic diseases had not been quantitatively reviewed previously.
